news.title: 'Devastating': Glee erupts as Susan Collins' 'road salt' boast blows up in her face
news.description: Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) bragged about a road salt win at a Maine Senate debate , and her challenger's comeback had observers cheering. On Tuesday, Collins faced Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in a debate weeks before the midterms. Asked what she would do about President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada , Collins pointed to a specific victory. "I was successful at getting road salt removed from the tariff list," Collins said. Jackson responded by pouncing on the answer. "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt," Jackson said. "With everything she's doing with the Iran war, there will be so many less people that can afford to drive that I'm not even sure the road salt will be worth anything." The exchange spread quickly after clips of the moment were posted, with many users zeroing in on Jackson's five-word retort. "'We can't eat road salt' is devastating," wrote Democratic political strategist Chris Sosa in a post on X. "I must report: 'You can't eat road salt' is a bar," laughed Democratic Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, referring to the term for a line of rap. Others compared Collins' answer to the infamous line attributed to Marie Antoinette. "Susan Collins' amazing let-them-eat-road-salt moment," declared journalist and political commentator David Sirota. "'Let them eat road salt.'—Susan Collins, basically," remarked disinformation expert and Kash Patel foe Jim Stewartson. Social media personality and liberal political commentator Brian Krassenstein marveled how "Troy Jackson just destroyed Susan Collins in 4 seconds." Some suggested the moment could have real consequences at the ballot box. "'We can't eat road salt' is the kind of line that could genuinely sway an election," warned policy consultant and journalist Adam Cochran. "Team Jackson has to be very happy with that soundbite." Author and activist Hemant Mehta framed the race around the exchange. "If cheaper road salt is what you want, vote Collins," he wrote . "If you want better health care and a real check on Trump and the Supreme Court, vote Jackson." "We can't eat road salt" is devastating. — Chris Sosa (@ChrisSosa) October 7, 2026

news.description: Onlookers were outraged Tuesday after Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) gave an underwhelming answer to a key question during the state's Senate debate. Collins faced off in a debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, where Collins was asked to defend her record supporting Trump's policies. At one time, the moderator asked Collins point-blank if Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh lied to her when he said he considered Roe v. Wade to be settled law, a case that he later sided with the conservative majority to overturn. "I do not feel that he lied, but I think he should not have said it is settled law," Collins said. "And to be fair, you can't ask a nominee how he might vote in some hypothetical future case." Collins' answer sparked a firestorm on social media. "Pathetic. He lied to your face and you rolled over like a dog," Adam Cochran, a policy analyst, posted on X. "You can’t 'feel' that someone lied or did not lie. news.title: Susan Collins hammered with corruption claims during Senate debate: 'I don't owe Trump'
news.description: Democrat Troy Jackson hammered Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) over a reported FBI corruption probe during their first debate Tuesday night. Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, laid out the allegations from a September ProPublica investigation as the two candidates clashed over Collins' ethics . "As late as 2024, the FBI was circling around Senator Collins," Jackson said. "They had emails, they knew about meetings. They've got a great big check for $150,000. It's a pay-to-play scheme involving her office and our taxpayer dollars. And then when Trump came back, his administration dismantled the investigation." He then tied Collins directly to the president. "Now, she votes with Donald Trump 96 percent of the time," Jackson said. "I don't owe Trump. I don't owe the billionaires. I've spent my life fighting back against billionaires, but I do owe the people of Maine everything." Collins again dismissed the ProPublica reporting as false, according to reporting by the Portland Press Herald, and Jackson kept pressing her on how the Trump administration ended the probe. Collins fired back by raising an ethics complaint a Republican lawmaker once filed against Jackson over his use of an Augusta home while he served in the Legislature. ProPublica reported that the head of a pro-Collins super PAC met with executives from Hawaii defense contractor Navatek in 2019 and asked for a $500,000 donation, the Bangor Daily News reported . Then-CEO Martin Kao sent $150,000 through a shell company and later told company executives in an internal email that Collins had committed to getting Navatek $32 million in Navy contracts. Kao is now in prison for money laundering, bank fraud, and defrauding the federal government, WBUR reported . An FBI spokesperson told ProPublica the bureau's earlier investigation found nothing implicating Collins or her campaign, Newsweek reported . During the debate, Jackson drove his point home, saying, "I refuse corporate PAC money. I want to ban congressional stock trading. I fight for Mainers every day. I'm not taking money from corporations like Senator Collins does."

news.title: Why the GOP’s Typical Attacks Aren’t Working on This Maine Candidate
news.description: You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free . Inside Washington Maine’s 2nd congressional district, covering 92 percent of the state, is the largest congressional district east of the Mississippi River. And right now, the largely rural, white population is getting ready to choose between two candidates: Democrat Matt Dunlap , who is a progressive and an avid hunter, or Republican and former two-term Governor Paul LePage , who once said “ tell them to kiss my butt ” when asked about criticism from the NAACP. In the race to replace Democratic Representative Jared Golden , who isn’t seeking reelection, polling is mixed. Dunlap, a member of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s, or DCCC, Red to Blue program supporting candidates in close races, was up six points in a University of New Hampshire poll from late September. Other surveys , however, show a dead heat or LePage slightly ahead. On Monday, Dunlap held a health care–focused press conference, amid a cost-of-living crisis exacerbated by the Trump administration’s war on Iran and tariff policies. These issues are a particularly powerful weapon against LePage, who vetoed Medicaid expansion six times as governor and called last year’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act “the greatest thing that can happen to the Maine people” (LePage was referring to the bill’s “no tax on tips” provision, but the legislation also cut Medicaid by nearly $1 trillion). Dunlap said that the cost of health care is one of the main issues he’s heard about from Mainers. In a conversation with The New Republic, he described a conversation with a resident who was considering selling their home to afford health care costs and another person whose insurance costs went from $560 to $2,700 per month when Affordable Care Act subsidies expired in December. Mainers are also worried about the cost of gas and heating oil, which could hurt LePage like it hurts every other Republican candidate in 2026. Maine is more reliant on heating oil than any other state in the country, and prices have skyrocketed this year. “The first frost warning for much of the state is tomorrow night, maybe tonight,” said Mark Brewer , the chair of the Political Science Department at the University of Maine, which is located in the second district. “It’s cold here. Winters are long here.” LePage has tried to distance himself somewhat from President Trump’s agenda. He came out against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods and has emphasized his focus on affordability as governor. The district is historically conservative, and voted for Trump all three times he was on the ballot. But, said Amy Fried , a retired professor of political science at the University of Maine, “This district is one where people are OK with splitting their tickets.” She explained that, in election years past, it wasn’t unusual to see houses with signs for Trump, GOP Senator Susan Collins , and Democratic Representative Jared Golden together in one yard. “Or pretty much any combination you could think of,” she added. Republicans in past elections have typically portrayed their opponents as out-of-touch leftists. So far, LePage has struggled to apply that playbook to Dunlap. “He doesn’t look like a wild-eyed radical in any way,” said Fried of Dunlap. “His personality is extremely even-keeled, and a friend of mine said the other day that he looks like an insurance salesman.” Asked about LePage recently telling Fox News Digital that the race is about “common sense versus crazy,” Dunlap seemed unfazed: “That’s what they say when they don’t have anything else to throw at you,” he told The New Republic. “MAGA Republicans,” Dunlap said, “are very good at demonizing and bringing up the wedge [issues] about the woke agenda and the Democratic Socialists of America.” But, he added, “I’m less susceptible to that because I hadn’t heard of the Democratic Socialists of America until we heard about the Mamdani campaign.” Dunlap has also played up his experience as a fisherman and hunter. He’s a founding board member of the Maine Youth Fish and Game Association, and the former executive director of the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine. One ad shows him fishing, boating, hunting, and shooting a rifle. At the end of the video, he puts down the gun and turns to the camera, saying: “I’ve always defended our Second Amendment rights, and in Congress, I’ll do the same.” “You can’t question his bona fides on outdoors kind of stuff, or guns,” said Brewer. “He can go toe-to-toe with any Republican on those issues.” Golden, who won this district four times, is a Marine Corps veteran who has similar credibility on guns, an important issue in the district. Both Brewer and Fried echoed what polls have suggested: This is a tight race that could go either way. Brewer said that much could hinge on the support that Dunlap gets from national Democrats in the next month. He pointed to the DCCC’s apparent hesitancy to add him to the Red to Blue program—Dunlap beat out the DCCC’s preferred candidate in June, but wasn’t added to the program until late August—as a potential issue. “The support still, to me, doesn’t seem like what it would be, or what it could be, or maybe should be in this tight of a race,” he said. “I think he could use some more money.” —Emma Janssen Outside Washington Early voting is now in progress across multiple states, having started on Monday in Maine , California , Nebraska , and Montana (although there it’s technically called a “late registration” period for absentee voting). New Mexico, Indiana, Wyoming, and Ohio begin on Tuesday, and Arizona starts on Wednesday. Early voting and early absentee voting (differentiated by whether a ballot is cast directly into a ballot counter) has been underway in Illinois and Minnesota for weeks. Several other states join next week. Pennsylvania technically doesn’t have early in-person voting, but it actually sort of does , since you can show up, get a mail-in ballot, and then hand it back. Voting rights advocates have typically urged people to vote early if possible, in part for convenience and to avoid lines , and in part so that there’s time to sort things out if there’s a problem. On Saturday, President Trump urged Republicans to vote early or by mail—measures he has previously opposed and tried to restrict. As key Senate and House races in Texas, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, Alaska, Ohio, and more continue to dominate headlines, fewer people are watching California. But over the weekend, Bernie Sanders stopped by California’s conservative Central Valley to give Democrat Randy Villegas a boost in his attempt to unseat David Valadao in the race for California’s 22nd district. Ever since Villegas’s victory over moderate, DCCC-backed Jasmeet Bains in the primary, part of the narrative in this race has focused on whether Villegas is too far left for this “historically conservative, low-turnout area,” as CalMatters puts it. But as Sanders’s visit shows, Villegas isn’t running away from his progressivism. Dems have been fixated on beating Valadao for years , so if a progressive is finally the one to do it, it’ll be quite the story. While public polling in the 22nd has been almost nonexistent this cycle, a Democratic PAC poll in June showed Villegas up four points . —Heather Souvaine Horn The Ideas Factory The Natural Resources Defense Council issued a statement on Suncor v. Boulder, the big climate case the Supreme Court heard oral arguments for on Monday. Suncor Energy is asking SCOTUS to throw out the suit from the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, over the devastating damages of climate change, including from the Marshall fire in 2021. “Coal, oil, and gas companies have made trillions of dollars in profits from the sale of fuels that are driving the climate crisis. They have knowingly misled the public for decades” and lobbied to delay climate policies, said NRDC senior vice president for environmental health Matthew Tejada . “Now a staggering bill is coming due.… The fossil fuel industry has a responsibility to help pay for the damage its products have caused.” On Wednesday at 4 p.m., the Center for Strategic and International Studies will host a webcast looking back at the anthrax postal attacks 25 years ago. Retired Maj. Gen. Paul Friedrichs will moderate a discussion between Wendi Kuhnert of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and former GOP Senator Richard Burr . On Thursday, the Institute for Policy Studies will hold its 50th annual Letelier-Moffitt Human Rights Awards, honoring Unidos MN and La Liga Sindical Obrera Mexicana for their work mobilizing “communities” to “defend their rights.” Unidos MN gained widespread recognition training people to document ICE abuses in Minnesota, and in recent months has shifted to getting out the vote for the midterm elections. La Liga, also known as the Mexican Workers’ League, is a relatively recent independent union—as opposed to the dominant so-called “ protection unions ” in Mexico that tend to favor employers’ interests . —Heather Souvaine Horn In Closing Four Questions For: Aaron Eisenberg , political director for United Auto Workers Region 9A Q: Who are you, and what are you working on right now? A: Region 9A represents 50,000 active and retired members across New York, New England, and Puerto Rico. After notching some amazing victories in New York this year, right now, our priorities are electing our former member Troy Jackson to the U.S. Senate in Maine, training our members to run campaigns and run for office, passing local and state legislation to strengthen worker power, winning unemployment for striking workers, and making it easier to unionize. Q: The UAW backed insurgent—and ultimately victorious—candidates like Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York primaries this year, while many established unions supported their opponents. What did the UAW understand about this political moment that others missed? A: In the last few years, we have had many strikes, pickets, and actions where we have called on politicians for their support. Those who showed up consistently in solidarity proved themselves to our members and earned their support in the future; those who did not were also remembered. Mayor Zohran Mamdani had been on the picket line with all eight of our UAW locals in New York City in the two years prior to his run. Claire Valdez was a unit chair in Local 2110 and was a UAW leader. Darializa Avila Chevalier was a leader within her public defense unit in Local 2325. Our members were ready to throw down for them as candidates when they ran. Q: Winning elections is one thing. How does the union ensure that union-backed candidates deliver for working people once in office? A: Everything we do, including endorsements, aims to build beyond elections. In New York City, we have now seen the fruits of this with the creation of the Mayor’s Office of Worker Power—an office that we and other allies proposed to the administration, and which will be led by a former UAW organizing director, Tony Perlstein. We are also in consistent dialogue with our elected champions to support our members during legislative fights and contract battles, as well as on specific issues like unemployment for striking workers, universal childcare, and Medicare for All. Q: What’s your favorite part about working in the labor movement? A: Waking up with a sense of purpose. We have an immense challenge in front of us, and yet the power of working people coming together has overcome insurmountable obstacles time and time again. Working with members, trusting people to grow, developing new leaders, and shifting power away from the billionaire class to a multiracial, working-class mass movement is the battle of our times, and I can think of no more worthy cause. They are entitled to a little representation, aren’t they, and a little chance?” Who was he? ( Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.) —Michael Tomasky
